questions.text: A student checks the data type of a variable that holds text (a value written in quotes) by running type(PAGENAME) in the interactive interpreter. What is printed?
questions.explanation: Verified: any value written in quotes is a string, so type() reports <class 'str'>. <class 'type'> is what you'd get from type(str), the type of a class itself.

questions.text: What value results from evaluating 10 // 3 in Python?
questions.explanation: Verified: 10 // 3 is 3. Floor division of two integers gives an integer, dropping the remainder. 3.0 would need a float operand, 3.33 is roughly true division, and 1 is the remainder (10 % 3).

questions.text: A parts list is stored as sample_list = ['part_1001', 'part_1002', 'part_1003', 'part_1004']. Which code accesses the second item in the list?
questions.explanation: Verified: sample_list[1] returns 'part_1002'. Indexing starts at 0, so [0] is the first item, [2] the third, and [-1] the last.

questions.text: A delivery system stores delivery_manifest = ["part_101", "part_240", "part_330", "part_999"]. What does delivery_manifest[-1] return?
questions.explanation: Verified: -1 counts back from the end, so it returns the last element, "part_999". Negative indexes are valid on any non-empty list, so there is no IndexError.

questions.text: A student is learning Python in interactive interpreter mode and issues the commands shown. What is the result of the last line?
questions.explanation: Verified: multiplying a string by an integer repeats it, so with y = 2 the result is 'TestTest'. The y*3 line before it only displays 6; it doesn't change y.

questions.text: A programmer's first condition is not met. Which Python keyword tests another condition and runs a different block if that one is true?
questions.explanation: elif ("else if") tests a new condition after the one above it fails. else takes no condition and just catches everything left over, while if else and then are not Python syntax.

questions.text: A script needs to import my_module, which is stored in /custom/path, a directory Python doesn't search by default. Which statement makes the module importable?
questions.explanation: Verified: sys.path is a plain list of directories searched on import, so it takes .append(); lists have no .add(). os.path is a module of path-string helpers, not the search list, and a bare path isn't defined.

questions.text: Which statement about Python's standard streams (sys.stdin / sys.stdout) is correct?
options: Command-line functions are preferred for stdout output.
open('file.txt', 'r') creates a read-only stream that processes standard input.
Standard streams are optimal for moving text through a program without loading file operations into memory.
questions.explanation: Standard streams pass text through as it arrives, line by line, so a script can filter a pipeline without reading a whole file into memory. open() creates a file object; it has nothing to do with sys.stdin. os.path only manipulates path strings, and process handling is os.popen() / subprocess.

questions.text: Custom exceptions such as NegativeNumberError are created by inheriting from the base Exception class.
questions.explanation: True. Verified: class NegativeNumberError(Exception): pass defines one, and it can be raised and caught like any built-in error, including by except Exception.

questions.text: A program runs int("Two Thousand"), which raises an error. Which except block catches it?
questions.explanation: Verified: it raises ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10. The argument is the right type (a string) but the wrong value. TypeError is for the wrong type, such as int([1]).

questions.text: An except Exception block catches a ValueError, because Exception sits above almost all runtime errors in the exception hierarchy.
questions.explanation: True. Verified: issubclass(ValueError, Exception) is True, and an except clause catches the named class and all of its subclasses.

questions.text: Which Linux command creates an empty file?
questions.explanation: touch file.txt creates the file if it doesn't exist (and only updates its timestamp if it does). make runs build rules from a Makefile, and create / new are not standard commands.

questions.text: A user runs mkdir testdir, then cd testdir, then systemctl status cron, then a systemctl set-default command. What is the current working directory afterwards?
questions.explanation: Only cd changes the working directory. systemctl talks to systemd and leaves the shell where it was, so the user is still in testdir. Outside Source cut off the set-default target, but it doesn't affect the answer.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the apt-get upgrade command?
options: Upgrades all installed packages to their latest versions
questions.explanation: upgrade installs newer versions of the packages already on the system. Refreshing the index is apt-get update, and clearing orphaned dependencies is apt-get autoremove.

questions.text: Which command uninstalls a package and also deletes its configuration files?
questions.explanation: purge removes the package and its config files. remove takes out the program but leaves the config behind, and delete / uninstall are not apt-get commands.

questions.text: Running sudo apt-get autoremove completely removes an installed package.
questions.explanation: False. autoremove takes no package name and only removes dependencies that were installed automatically and are no longer needed by anything. To fully remove a specific package and its config, use sudo apt-get purge <package>. Note: Outside Source says True, but it's keyed False here for the reason above. If the course insists on True, raise it with the instructor.
questions.warning: Outside Source says True. It's keyed False here because autoremove only clears unused dependencies. If the real quiz grades it True, take it up with the instructor.

questions.text: A script defines a global multiplier = 5, and inside multiply_number(num) it assigns a local multiplier = 10 before returning num * multiplier. When the function runs, the interpreter prioritizes the global value (5).
questions.explanation: False. Verified: multiply_number(10) returns 100, and the global is still 5 afterwards. Name lookup checks the local scope first, so the local multiplier shadows the global inside the function. The global is only used when the function never assigns that name.

questions.text: A script sorts device names into two lists using the code shown. What is the value of switches after the loop runs?
questions.context:
devices = ["RT1", "RT2", "RT3", "SW1", "SW2", "SW3"] + ["RT4", "SW4"]
routers = []
switches = []
for i in devices:
    if "R" in i:
        routers.append(i)
    else:
        switches.append(i)
questions.explanation: Verified by running it: switches is ['SW1', 'SW2', 'SW3', 'SW4']. Every name containing R (including RT4) goes to routers. The SW names are appended in list order, and SW4 comes last because it sits at the end of the concatenated list. Outside Source only described this code in words, so the snippet was rebuilt from that description.

questions.text: Running pip install requests works because PIP is the standard package manager that connects to the Python Package Index (PyPI).
questions.explanation: True. PIP downloads packages from PyPI, the public repository of third-party Python libraries, and installs them into the current environment.

questions.text: Which Python feature relies on yield to produce values on the fly using lazy evaluation?
questions.explanation: Verified: a function containing yield returns a generator object, which hands back one value per iteration instead of building the whole sequence in memory.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about object-oriented programming in Python are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: Redefining a method such as take_damage() in a subclass such as Knight demonstrates polymorphism.
A class is the blueprint; an object is an instance of that class.
Procedural programming relies on encapsulating state and methods inside classes rather than step-by-step functions.
Creating a child class such as Car that inherits from a parent class such as Vehicle demonstrates inheritance.
An object encapsulates both data (properties) and behavior (methods).
questions.explanation: The third statement has it backwards: encapsulating state and methods inside classes is what object-oriented programming does, and procedural programming is the step-by-step function style. The rest are accurate. Overriding a method in a subclass is polymorphism, a class is the blueprint for its instances, subclassing is inheritance, and objects bundle data with behavior.

questions.text: Running grep 'd..m' /etc/passwd works because each dot matches exactly one character, so it finds daem in daemon and dnsm in dnsmasq.
questions.explanation: True. Verified: in a regex, . matches any single character, so d..m is a four-character pattern (d, any two characters, m). Running it against daemon and dnsmasq matched daem and dnsm.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about grep commands and regular-expression behavior are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: grep 'new*' /etc/passwd only matches the exact four-letter word news.
grep 'd..m' /etc/passwd uses dots as wildcards to match patterns like daem and dnsm.
grep '^root' /etc/passwd uses ^ to match root only at the beginning of a line.
grep 'false$' /etc/passwd uses $ to match lines where false is at the end.
questions.explanation: Verified: new* also matched nonexistent, because * repeats the preceding w zero or more times, so plain ne is enough. That makes the first statement wrong. The dot, ^ and $ statements are all correct.

questions.text: In vi, pressing a in command mode inserts text at the cursor's current position.
questions.explanation: False. a appends: insert mode starts just after the cursor. i is the key that inserts at the cursor's current position.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about package administration on the DEVASC VM are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: apt-cache search speed test searches package descriptions locally without needing administrative privileges.
sudo apt-get purge speedtest-cli removes the package along with its configuration files.
Installing a new package requires root access via sudo apt-get install <package_name>.
sudo apt-get update updates all installed packages to their latest versions.
questions.explanation: update only refreshes the list of available packages; upgrade is the command that installs newer versions, so the last statement is wrong. apt-cache search reads the local package cache and needs no sudo, purge also deletes config files, and installing writes to system directories, so it needs root.
